Title: Deck limitations at GenCon (sanctioned VTES tournament)

Messages.Author: J. Hunter Johnson
Messages.Body:
I was at GenCon this past weekend, and signed up for the VTES Sanctioned
Tournament (i.e., the one being run by WotC).

At the beginning of the tournament (actually, about 10 minutes after it
was supposed to have begun) a WotC rep announced the deck limitations --
no ante cards and no more than four of any given card! Players were
given about 15 minutes to tweak their decks.

I only had a my deck with me (no extra cards), and it had 5-8 copies of
some cards. So I dropped out before play began.

This would seem like good info to disseminate *before* the convention.

Hunter

Messages.Author: CurtAdams
Messages.Body:
jhun...@io.com (J. Hunter Johnson) writes:

>I was at GenCon this past weekend, and signed up for the VTES Sanctioned
>Tournament (i.e., the one being run by WotC).

>At the beginning of the tournament (actually, about 10 minutes after it
>was supposed to have begun) a WotC rep announced the deck limitations --
>no ante cards and no more than four of any given card! Players were
>given about 15 minutes to tweak their decks.

Three possibilities on this one, all of them bad:

1) There was nobody to run the Jyhad tournament. They hauled in some
Magic tournament official who didn't know any better. (My favorite
explanation; this indicates only lack of interest, or, if we're really
lucky, just an untimely epidemic affecting the WotC Jyhad staff)

2) Somebody clued them in on the power of the untap cards or the severity
of the vote-pushing misrule. They threw on the 4-card limit in a
desperate attempt to fix things, not realizing that, while Freak Drive and
pushable KRC's create broken decks, 4-card limits make Jyhad come apart at
the seams and create a broken GAME.

3) They've completely lost it.

Gracious, even if you did want to impose card limits in Jyhad (a bad idea)
you wouldn't want 4. You need at least 15% rushes (6 Bum's Rushes and 6
Haven Uncovered in an 80-card deck) for operational rush decks and at
least 10% bleed bounce for Ventrue vote decks (8 Deflections in an 80-card
deck). Less those decks, there is no Jyhad game. There's a lot of other
decks that need certain cards in large numbers to deal with certain
tricks, but those 2 are essential to prevent Jyhad: the Malkavianade.

Incidentally, I played at a tournament run by somebody who'd almost been a
victim of my Freaky Bleed deck at the one tournament I played it. He
decided to install 4-card limits. I sat down and built, on the spot, one
of these boring 4-of-every-stealth and 4-of-every-bleed and
4-of-every-card-you-want-in-a-Malk/Tremere-dominated-game Malk decks (I
normally don't play such things). In the first round, I simply plowed
through a table of 2 players trying to play non-Malk decks (functional
concepts, both of them, but they had no chance with 4-card) and a beginner
Malk deck crippled by a lack of access to rare and uncommon cards
(normally also functional, but, again, not with card limits). The second
round never happened, partly as there were some scheduling conflicts, and
partly as it was judged unlikely anybody could catch me. The tournament
director does NOT intend to use card limits for his next tournament, thank
god.

>I only had a my deck with me (no extra cards), and it had 5-8 copies of
>some cards. So I dropped out before play began.

Boy, what a bummer. I'm now carrying around that Malkavian monstrosity
deck just in case I run into 4-card somewhere.

>This would seem like good info to disseminate *before* the convention.

Anybody who wishes to depart from standard tournament rules must announce
it in advance, even if it's for a very good reason. I would think this
particularly true of the company that published the tournament rules, but
maybe I'm just old-fashioned :-)

Curt Adams (curt...@aol.com)

newsgroup to make them make a saner decision and we couldn't have *that*.
I made it to the finals and had the eventual winner down to 1 pool (he
woke twice and deflected 2 Day Operation bleeds from a Famed vampire in
the same turn-->I Freak Drived the Famed vamp on his way to torpor and
rescued him for the second Day Op bleed). And guess what?! The champ was
playing a Malkavian

points determining who would play in the final round. (I got skunked in

Messages.Author: Shane Travis
Messages.Body:
sab...@cwo.com wrote:
: The card limit just forces you to

: get more creative with your combos instead of relying on KRC, Majesty
: and other overused cards.

I don't think that you will find anyone on this group who will argue that
both Majesty and KRC are undervalued/overused/abused cards (along with
some others, i.e. WWEF), BUT the main thrust of no-limit arguments is
that there is no point limiting over 98% of the cards because 2% are
improperly made.

Limits on specific (broken) cards - sure. Limits based on a percentage
of deck size - more objectionable, but still playable. To lift whole
cloth a card limit from a game that was never designed to be played
without limits without even really examining the issue is rather silly.

Magic was originally designed with two inherent limits. It was expected
that people would spend about as much on the game as they would with any
other RPG/Wargame ($30-$75), and it was designed to be played for Ante:
in this way, all-common decks would win less-often but take more valuable
cards from more powerful, rare-dependent decks. When it became obvious
that neither of these laboratory conditions carried over to the real
world, it became quickly obvious that the game was broken. The 4-card
limit was designed to circumvent this breakage.

Jyhad was designed (by all external evidence) to fit together as a
cohesive whole, and not to need card limits. Granted, a few mistakes
were made and a few bad rulings have been made by the DT, but generally,
the game works better without card limits than with them.

If you don't think so, try anything other than a Malkavian S&B deck
against Curt's aforementioned 4-card monster. I'll lay odds as to who
comes out on top...

>Back to the issue: Malk decks dont tend to last long in our group.

>a few turns.

Well,if the whole table can efficaciously gang up on one player, that will
stop just about anything. But, as I read in another discussion somewhere,
that just proves the power of the deck - nobody has a chance against it
alone.

> The problem card we see with no limits is Majesty. A
>Toreador deck with loads of these would be about THE most annoying
>deck I would ever have to face.

You're right on Majesty - it's a "whoops" card. But the solution is to
recost Majesty (I recommend adding a blood cost of one) or, if worst comes
to worst, restricting Majesty. The power of Majesty is no reason to
restrict Dodge.

Incidentally, the whole table ganging up will toast a no-limits Majestic
Bleed at least as well as a Malk Bleed under 4-card. One Brujah rush deck
in the game and it's Sayonara, Mr. Majesty.

There are a couple of "whoops" cards about (about a dozen, IMO), and
there's been a lot of discussion here on which they are and how to fix
them. But the problem cards give reason to restrict or change the problem
cards, and are no reason to restrict any other card in the game.

I'm of the opinion that a Ventrue Majesty deck is scarier that a Toreador,
although both would be pretty bad.

P.S. "Magnamious" isn't the right word. I suspect you meant "monstrous"
:-) But we all know what you meant.
Curt Adams (curt...@aol.com)

- e.g., Wolf Claws for Bum's Rush. The majority of good non-$$$ deck need
at least 8 of at least one card.

If Wizards sticks on 4-card limits to patch up holes they created or chose
not to fix, we may have to. I don't think they are that clueless, though.

>>of these boring 4-of-every-stealth and 4-of-every-bleed and
^^^^^
>Here is were some people differ,I think that playing with 10 different
>cards is boring, Yeah they have there neat little combos,but wear thin
>quite quickly.

Ah you're denying yourself one of the great pleasures of Jyhad play. In
Jyhad, the combos don't wear thin.

In many card games, the limit on what you can do comes from what you've
been lucky enough to draw. Draw a combo, it goes off. Effectively you
play against Lady Luck and your own deck construction rules.

In Jyhad, if you want a combo, you can arrange for it to be fairly
reliable. What stops you is not luck or deck construction rules - it is
the other players, spinning their own webs and combos. Believe me, they
are far more capable and interesting opponents than luck or deck
construction rules. You get a fascinating environment where decks and
players evolve against each other. As Richard Dawkins points out,
evolution is much more interesting when things evolve against each other
than when they evolve against external limits.

>>Boy, what a bummer. I'm now carrying around that Malkavian monstrosity
>>deck just in case I run into 4-card somewhere.

>Any skilled player can design a deck to counter a Malk bleed deck.

Without limits, sure. With limits, only the Tremere.

Mostly the latter. Almost all Jyhad cards as printed are fine, in that
they all have different strengths and weaknesses, or advantages in
specific situations and weaknesses in others. Some of the 'whoops' cards
above are such that there is (almost) no conceivable situation where they

WotC came up with the fix for it that it did - and now it is no longer a
'whoops' card.

Messages.Author: Dennis Jeffery Murphy
Messages.Body:
Heya,

My group plays without limits or problems.

One of the things I enjoy about a no-limit rule is fear. No one knows for
sure what's, left in your library, ever. Last night I played a five hour,
three-player game. I was gangrel, they were Malk, Brujah, Tremere, and
Toreador. The bluffs that were going on were brutal!

With a four card limit, it's easy to tell when someone's run out of
Wakes, or Majesties, or Claws, or whatever. It's great to watch your
opponents sweat as they consider their next move. It's great to sweat
yourself! And it's divine to finally actually have the combo your
opponent thinks you have, just when he or she decides to perform that
critical move...

In Halifax we refer to Jyhad as a sort of "Blame Game". The decks just
don't seem to be as crucial to the game as the play, and if a person
loses, the blame is easily traced back to an error they made.

In terms of tourneys, the drag about having more than 4 of each card is
tweaking your deck as you go. I usually make an engine of 40 or 50 cards,
trying to adhere to a 4 card formula, and then make 10 card add-ons, so I
don't go mad or run out of cards if 2 or 3 more people show up. Like that
game last night. I needed every card in that deck, and all our libraries
were empty before we finished. Nasty!

Stay outta the sun,
